item.title: I tried 4 open-source launchers on my Pixel, and settled on the most underrated one
item.itunes:title: I tried 4 open-source launchers on my Pixel, and settled on the most underrated one
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The Pixel is known for its clean Android experience, but its default launcher isn't the only way to use your home screen. I wanted to see what open-source alternatives could offer, so I tried four launchers that take different approaches to Android. Some focus on reducing distractions, while others rethink how I find and organize apps. I wasn't looking for endless customization options or flashy features. I wanted a launcher that felt right for everyday use. After testing all four on my Pixel, one option stood out for reasons I didn't quite expect.

Escape Launcher

This launcher asked me to slow down

Escape Launcher felt like a different kind of experiment on my Pixel. Instead of giving me another traditional Android home screen to customize, it takes a more minimal approach to how I interact with my phone. The idea is to reduce the distractions that come with constantly seeing app icons, widgets, and other things competing for my attention.

What stood out to me was how different it felt from the setup I was used to. I didn't have the same familiar home screen filled with shortcuts to fall back on, so using the launcher required a small adjustment. That change was interesting, especially when I wanted to see how far I could simplify my everyday phone experience.

However, I also realized that this approach wasn't an ideal fit for how I use my Pixel. I like having some control over my home screen, and I didn't want to sacrifice that convenience just to make things look simpler. Escape Launcher was an interesting starting point, but I wanted to try a few more options before settling on one.

Kvaesitso

A search-first launcher with a bit of a learning curve

Kvaesitso was probably the most unusual launcher I tried on my Pixel. It takes a search-first approach instead of relying on the usual home screen and app drawer layout. Instead of organizing everything around app icons, it encourages me to search for what I need and go there directly. This felt like a practical idea, especially when I couldn't remember where I had placed a particular app.

I also liked that Kvaesitso goes beyond basic app searching. Its widgets and search integrations give me ways to access useful information without opening several different apps. Once I started exploring its options, I could see why it appeals to people who want more control over how they navigate Android.

I have spent years using conventional launchers, so changing those habits wasn't always natural. I sometimes wanted to tap an app icon instead of searching for it. Kvaesitso has plenty to offer, but I wasn't convinced that a search-focused interface was the right fit for my daily routine. I moved on to Olauncher to see whether a simpler approach would work better.

4 Google apps I replace on every new Android phone, and every replacement is free

A new Android phone gets four immediate replacements, and they don't cost me anything.

2
By  Yash Patel

Olauncher

I enjoyed the clean look at first

Olauncher took minimalism in a different direction on my Pixel. Its text-based home screen replaces the usual grid of colorful app icons with a much simpler layout. I could see only the apps I chose to keep on the home screen, without a wall of icons taking up space. It was a refreshing change, and I liked how little visual clutter there was whenever I unlocked my phone.

Setting it up was straightforward. I selected my preferred apps and arranged them on the home screen, keeping the ones I used most often within easy reach. The lack of unnecessary elements made the interface feel clean, and I didn't need to spend much time adjusting its appearance before I could start using it.

Still, Olauncher wasn't quite what I wanted as a permanent replacement. I enjoy the flexibility of Android, and the stripped-down interface felt limiting when I wanted a more personalized setup. It does its job well if minimalism is your priority, but I missed having more options to make the home screen feel like my own.

Lawnchair

Keeping the Pixel feel, adding more control

Lawnchair felt like a natural fit for my Pixel because it builds on the familiar Android experience instead of completely changing how I use my phone. I could keep the home screen layout I was comfortable with while getting more freedom to customize its appearance. After trying launchers with very different approaches, this balance was a welcome change.

I liked having control over details such as icon styles, grid layout, and other home screen settings. These options let me personalize my setup without spending too much time figuring out how everything worked. The interface also felt familiar enough that I could get started quickly without changing my usual habits. Lawnchair gave me room to experiment. I could try different layouts and visual styles until I found something that suited my preferences.

I install these 5 open-source apps on every Pixel before anything else

A new Pixel is great out of the box, but these open-source apps make it even better.

2
By  Yash Patel

Sometimes, the best launcher is the one that just gets it right

Trying these four launchers reminded me that the best home screen isn't necessarily the one with the most features or the most unusual design. Each offers something different, depending on how you use your phone. For me, Lawnchair strikes the right balance between customization and familiarity. It gives me enough freedom to make my Pixel feel more personal without overcomplicating things. Sometimes, that's all I need from a launcher.

Lawnchair

item.title: I replaced Apple Notes, Google Keep, and OneNote with Obsidian, and its biggest mobile flaw is finally gone
item.itunes:title: I replaced Apple Notes, Google Keep, and OneNote with Obsidian, and its biggest mobile flaw is finally gone
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
For most of us, our notes are divided between two or more apps and we don't really think twice about it. A case in point is the average phone which will have a hodgepodge of Apple Notes, Google Keep, and OneNote. Those come with the hardware or the Google and Microsoft accounts that are already active. That's fine for capturing quick thoughts, but it can be hard to make sense of one afterwards when it's in an app by itself and the context is somewhere else.

If the goal is to put everything in one pot, Obsidian is a very decent option. Its desktop app has been my go-to for a while now, and I also more recently started using the mobile app. But the mobile version is where the promise wanes. There is something about it that drives people back to the very apps they wanted to abandon, and that's the inability for quick capture on certain devices. Well, Obsidian finally fixed it.

Obsidian still beats the apps with proprietary formats

It doesn't lock you in

Apple Notes, Google Keep, and OneNote all keep your notes inside the app itself. Obsidian saves everything as plain Markdown files in a folder on your device, so any text editor can open them. If Obsidian disappeared tomorrow, the notes would still be safe and sound in that folder.

Google Keep is probably one of the tools I leaned on most for quick capture because it's pretty fast and easy to navigate most of the time, so I'll give it that. At the same time, it has no folders or subfolders, just labels, and you can only have 50 labels. Mine turned into one long scroll of colored cards that I ended up searching through instead of actually browsing, which got old pretty quickly.

OneNote at least has real structure, but it stores notes in only a format Microsoft can read, and there's still no Markdown export as of 2026. Apple Notes picked up Markdown export with iOS 26, which is a nice addition, but that conversion only happens when you export or import - the rest of the time your notes aren't in Markdown at all, and the app is still built around Apple's devices.

This type of lock-in is the exact reason why so many switch over to local options like Obsidian - not only are your notes not exactly private, but you have a couple of export and conversion steps to go through. Obsidian gets around a lot of that with its own importer, which handles all three apps and turns each note into a Markdown file in your vault.

I replaced Notion, Google Tasks, and Figma with one Obsidian setup, and now I can’t go back

I built my perfect productivity hub

1
By  Parth Shah

Obsidian had a mobile problem

But it finally got fixed

Obsidian on a phone has always had a bit of a UX problem. Tapping the app kicks off a whole loading sequence for your vault and plugins before you can actually type. And the larger your vault is, the longer the wait.

It isn't an iPhone thing, either. The Obsidian forums have years of threads about slow starts on both platforms, like an Android user whose 213-file vault was taking around 11 seconds just to read its files. Over on iOS, people describe a blank screen after the system puts the app to sleep. There are many of these types of reports, and most of them pretty much matched my own issue with the app too. So, quick notes ended up going to Google Keep or Apple Notes.

Obsidian's answer to this was Quick Capture. It was released in early access in September, then went public with 1.14 in October. On iOS 26, it lets you write a note from the Lock Screen, Control Center, Home Screen widgets, or Shortcuts without waiting for the vault to load. The catch is that it's iPhone-only for now. Android's part of 1.14 was smaller, including an Open Note widget that now shows the note's name.

I use Obsidian all the time, but this free, self-hosted notes app might be even better

If you're looking for an Obsidian alternative, Blinko is the best I've used so far.

6
By  Adam Conway

How Quick Capture transformed my Obsidian workflow on mobile

I don't have Sync, which makes it the perfect workflow for Quick Capture

You can start by setting it up in the control center, which now has a set of Obsidian controls, including Quick Note, New Note, Daily Note, and Search. Quick Note is the one you want for this quick capture setup. Add your picks as their own controls, and hitting any one of them will take you straight to the Obsidian app.

Quick Note, specifically, opens an empty screen with a "your new thought…" prompt and the keyboard already up - Obsidian says it launches faster than the iOS animation takes to finish. If I lock the phone halfway through, the note stays reachable through a Live Activity on the Lock Screen and Dynamic Island.

Where the capture goes depends on Locations, which you pick from a button at the top of that screen. A Location gets a name and a vault, then a Behavior. The behavior dictates whether the capture becomes its own note or gets added to something (either today's daily note or a specific note you pick). Optional settings cover the folder and template, plus a toggle to open the note after capturing, and titles are automatic by default, which in my case meant the date and time stamped on the front. Mine is called Inbox and makes a new note every time.

I don't pay for Obsidian Sync, so my phone vault has never matched my desktop vaults, which meant I never used Obsidian on my phone nearly as much. Now that the user experience is much quicker, I have no reason not to use it. Every capture is a plain Markdown file, so getting the useful ones onto my PC simply involves capturing them quickly on my phone, then transferring them to myself when I have time.

4 game-changing Obsidian workflows I wish I tried earlier

Obsidian workflows I tried late, but you don’t have to

4
By  Parth Shah

My phone vault finally stopped collecting dust

Funny thing is, the update didn't touch much of what people actually like about Obsidian. The editor is the same, and the links and plugins all work how they always did. I think the slow start was the main reason three other apps were in my rotation in the first place. Quick Notes really changed the note-taking game for me on mobile - Android users are still waiting on their version, and hopefully that doesn't take too long.

Free normally; $4/month for Obsidian Sync

item.title: Steam is a better way to run Windows apps on Linux than Wine, and it's not just for games
item.itunes:title: Steam is a better way to run Windows apps on Linux than Wine, and it's not just for games
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
It feels like more people than ever want to leave Windows behind and switch to Linux, but the biggest issue that has always plagued the platform is still a big hurdle. Many of the biggest Windows apps don't have Linux versions, and tools like Wine are still a requirement to make them work.

Steam addressed a big portion of this problem — that is, gaming — with its Proton compatibility layer, but what you may not realize is that it doesn't have to be just for games. You can use Steam to make all kinds of Windows apps run on Linux, and in many ways, it's a better option than Wine itself.

Proton is Wine, but better

Most of the time, at least

It's not exactly news at this point, but Valve's Proton layer is heavily based on Wine. The company took that open-source solution, built upon it, and then contributed many of those improvements back to Wine, which helps make the whole ecosystem better.

However, not every feature built into Proton makes its way back to the main Wine project, and if it does, it may take some time before that happens. Wine is a separate project with its own approval process for new submissions, so it's not necessarily in lockstep with whatever progress Valve makes at any given time.

Wine has been translating Windows games to Linux since 1993, but Proton is what made it effortless

Wine is the foundation that makes gaming on Linux possible.

8
By  Adam Conway

As such, running your programs under Proton can still be beneficial over using a plain Wine installation. Technically, some regressions are also possible, but most of the time, you're working with a version of Wine that's been improved upon by a company that has a direct financial incentive to do a good job of it.

Steam can even replace Bottles

A more configurable experience

When you install Wine on Linux, that's just kind of what it is. Wine creates the Windows filesystem so it can closely replicate the original functionality of your apps, and every Windows app you install after that uses that same file system. It mostly works fine, but much like Proton itself, new versions of Wine can sometimes have regressions in specific software and cause things to break.

A well-known solution for this has been Bottles, which lets you create isolated, single-use environments for each Windows app, with different Wine versions and configuration options. But Steam can do that too, albeit to a lesser extent.

When you install a Windows application using Steam, the Windows filesystem is created all over again for that specific app, allowing it to function independently of other apps, and crucially, giving you the option to run it with more specific settings. You don't get all the setup options Bottles gives you if you want to get really deep into it, but Steam lets you choose the compatibility layer you want to use for that app, including various versions of Proton and the Steam Linux Runtime. If an app depends on other apps, you can technically also install additional software to the same Windows filesystem, which can replicate some of the features Bottles offers.

Setting up is easy

Steam handles the hard part

If you're wondering how this all even works, it's actually fairly easy. First, you'll naturally need Steam on your Linux PC, and from the Steam menu, you can select Games and then Add non-Steam game to my library. Assuming you've already downloaded the installer for the Windows program you want to use, simply select the executable for said installer.

In this window, you can use the Compatibility tab to choose the compatibility layer you want to use. Steam defaults to Proton Experimental, which should give you the latest fixes and improvements, but you can switch to the stable release or one of the many earlier releases, or even other forks of Proton that focus on specific improvements. If you don't know what to try first, Proton Experimental is probably a fine choice, but you can play around with it if you have issues. The internet may also be able to provide specific recommendations for each app.

Linux gaming is getting faster because Windows APIs are becoming Linux kernel features

As time goes on, fewer games than ever are unplayable on Linux

18
By  Ty Sherback

From there, run the program through Steam and allow it to install. The more challenging part comes next, because Steam will keep pointing to the installer, not the actual app, so you have to find it yourself. Files for Windows apps in Steam are installed to this folder:

~/.local/share/Steam/steamapps/compatdata/

While you won't see any names here, you should be able to find your app by opening the most recent folder here, and then browse the structure to pfx/drive_c, and from there, check either Program Files or Program Files (x86) (or whatever the installation path would be) to find the executable for the actual app.

With that information, go back to Steam, right-click the program you installed, and select Properties. Under target, paste the full path to the executable file for the program you want. Under Start in, paste the path to the folder where the file is, essentially just removing the name of the executable itself from the path above. After that, starting the app in Steam should launch your Windows program normally going forward.

A benefit of this approach is that since app also creates its own Windows filesystem, the files never have a chance to interfere with each other or muddle up the Windows "installation". If you're done with a specific app, you can remove it from Steam and delete its respective folder to cleanly remove all of its Windows data without breaking any other Windows apps.

How well does it really work?

Don't expect miracles

As great as Steam is for this, it's important to remember it won't make miracles happen. Proton won't fix every single Windows app that doesn't work with Wine. My first experiments were me throwing curveballs at this setup with apps I usually know don't work. Clip Studio Paint installed but would crash upon launch, Obsbot Center seemed to work until I plugged in a webcam that would actually use it, at which point it crashed, and Microsoft 365 refused to install altogether. All of that is pretty much as expected with Wine, too.

However, simpler apps did work. Notepad++ was the best example, as it looked and run just about as perfectly as I could have hoped. I also tried installing the Vivaldi web browser (despite it having a Linux version), mostly because I wanted to see if it would be able to use my webcam, which it was. I was able to join a Discord call and use my camera, though I wasn't able to see anyone else on the call. Other users did say they were able to see me, though.

Otherwise, the experience can be a little hit or miss, but thankfully, having multiple compatibility options helps address that. For example, when using Proton, Vivaldi and OnlyOffice had an issue where the KDE window frame was trying to render around the Windows app and breaking the UI, but I could switch the compatibility to the Legacy Steam Runtime, and it worked just like Wine does. That flexibility can help some apps run better.

I thought I needed Windows for Photoshop, but this Linux project is just as good

Affinity on Linux is a game changer

13
By  João Carrasqueira

Finally, I tried Affinity and even the installer refused to launch. Interestingly, it does launch and install under Wine, though the app then fails to run anyway. The only way I've been able to get Affinity to work is through the dedicated Affinity on Linux project, which does a lot more setup to get things working. Even then, it's a finicky app.

Steam is a great way to manage Windows apps

Valve has already changed the way Windows games run on Linux with Proton, but it's great to see that Steam can do even more for all kinds of apps. It basically becomes its own Windows emulator with multiple compatibility options, and you can more easily manage the filesystem. It's not quite on the level of something like Bottles in terms of flexibility, but it still works very well and it's an app you're probably already used to launching anyway.

item.title: I replaced my $20 ChatGPT and Claude subscriptions with local AI to cut costs, but it backfired
item.itunes:title: I replaced my $20 ChatGPT and Claude subscriptions with local AI to cut costs, but it backfired
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
AI subscriptions can get expensive when you're paying for more than one service. With open-weight models becoming increasingly capable, I started wondering whether I could get similar results without paying monthly fees. Since I already had a powerful PC, running AI locally seemed like a practical way to cut costs. I decided to give it a proper try to see how far I could get without relying on paid AI services. What I discovered wasn't quite what I expected. Local AI had plenty of advantages, but replacing cloud services turned out to be more complicated than simply downloading a model and running it.

I wanted to stop paying for ChatGPT and Claude every month

My plan to stop paying for AI

Paying for both ChatGPT and Claude every month started to feel like an expense I could avoid. I liked having access to capable AI models, but I wasn't convinced I needed to keep paying for two separate services when open-weight models were becoming increasingly capable.

I've always enjoyed experimenting with self-hosted software, so running AI locally seemed like a natural next step. I wanted to see whether it could handle my AI needs without another monthly bill. The idea was simple: stop paying for subscriptions, use the hardware I already owned, and take greater control over how I accessed AI.

Setting up my local AI stack was easier than I expected

I had local AI running in minutes

  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 

Getting started with local AI was more straightforward than I expected. I used Ollama to download and run models on my PC without dealing with a complicated setup. Once it was running, switching between models was as simple as pulling a different one and loading it.

I also set up Open WebUI to get a familiar chat interface in my browser. It made interacting with local models feel much closer to using a regular AI chatbot, rather than working with command-line tools.

I experimented with several models on my RTX 5070 machine, although their performance and resource requirements differed. I liked being able to try different models without signing up for another service or worrying about subscription-plan usage limits. Getting everything running was easy.

I discovered the hidden costs of running AI locally

The costs I didn't see coming

The biggest surprise was realizing that running AI locally wasn't entirely free. I already owned a PC, so I didn't have to spend money on new hardware, but that didn't mean running models came without ongoing costs. My RTX 5070 draws additional power when handling demanding workloads, and frequent AI sessions can add to my electricity bill.

There was also the cost of time. I spent time downloading different models, checking their requirements, and figuring out which ones worked best for my needs. Larger models also consumed more system resources, making it harder to run other demanding applications alongside them.

None of these expenses looked significant on their own, but they made the savings less straightforward than I had imagined. I had removed the subscription fees, but I hadn't eliminated the costs of accessing AI. My cheaper alternative wasn't as cheap as it first appeared.

Ollama is the easiest way to start with local AI, and it's also the first thing I'd replace

Ollama made local AI easy, but I found a reason to leave it behind.

1
By  Yash Patel

Local AI couldn't replace everything I used cloud AI for

Free models couldn't do it all

The biggest limitation became clear when I tried to rely on local models for everything. They handled many straightforward requests well, but the results weren't always consistent when I needed more detailed reasoning or nuanced answers. Sometimes, I had to rephrase my prompts several times or verify the output before I could use it.

I also noticed a difference in how well models followed complex instructions. A response that needed little correction from ChatGPT or Claude could require more manual work when I used a local alternative. That extra effort mattered, especially when I wanted to finish a task quickly.

I could have continued switching between models until I found the right one for every request, but that would have defeated part of the purpose. I wanted a practical replacement, not another thing to manage. Local AI was useful, but expecting it to replace both subscriptions completely was unrealistic.

I stopped chasing savings and switched to a hybrid AI workflow

My hybrid AI setup finally made sense

Eventually, I stopped trying to replace every paid AI service with a local model. Instead, I started looking at which option made the most sense for each task. I kept local AI available for requests where it delivered good results, and I could avoid sending every prompt to an external service.

For more demanding tasks, I was willing to use cloud AI when the difference in output quality justified the cost. This way, I didn't have to compromise just to avoid a monthly payment. I could also reconsider whether I needed both subscriptions instead of automatically renewing them.

The experience changed how I think about saving money with self-hosted tools. Free software is great, but the real value depends on how well it fits my workflow. I didn't eliminate every AI expense, but I found a more practical balance between cost, convenience, and control.

I ditched $20 ChatGPT subscription and made Claude and Gemini work together for better results

What happens when you stop asking one AI to do everything and let two models collaborate?

8
By  Yash Patel

Free isn't always cheaper

Experimenting with local AI helped me understand what my hardware could handle and gave me more control over my AI setup. But I also learned that avoiding a subscription isn't the same as saving money. Hardware, electricity, time, and the quality of results all matter when deciding what's worth paying for.

If you're considering making the same switch, don't cancel your subscriptions just because local models are free. Try them alongside your existing tools first. You might discover that local AI is all you need, or that a combination of free and paid tools makes more sense.

Landing pages. Mobile applications. SaaS platforms. B2B software. Personal portfolios. Learning management systems. E-commerce websites. Productivity tools. Customer relationship management (CRM) systems. Content management systems. Browser extensions. Project management tools.

These are just some of the things most people have traditionally associated with coding and programming. That includes me too! For the longest time, coding has largely been viewed as a way to build something functional, whether that's a website, an application, or a piece of software designed to solve a particular problem users have been frustrated with forever.

However, something I've now realized is that there's a whole other side to coding (more specifically, vibe coding) that I had never considered before. Let me explain what I really mean by that...

Coding has turned into a form of self-expression

My favorite builds aren't necessarily useful

One of my favorite AI builders, Zara Zhang, has been advocating for something I've started to think about a lot lately: the idea that coding is becoming a form of self-expression.

She explains that coding is no longer just a way to build functional software. Instead, it's becoming a medium through which people can express their creativity, share their perspectives, and turn their imagination into something others can actually experience.

She goes as far as comparing vibe coding to traditional forms of creative expression, like writing, painting, and filmmaking. The goal with all of these mediums has never primarily been to create something useful. Instead, the process of creating something can be just as meaningful as the finished product itself.

Zhang says that when someone uses software you've built, they're essentially seeing the world through your lens, even if it's just for a brief moment. She explains in an X post that they're also temporarily adopting your mental models, or essentially the way you think, approach problems, and make sense of the world, to accomplish something. In a way, the software you build becomes a reflection of how your mind works.

You can vibe-code literally anything

My imagination is doing all the heavy lifting now

All of the above has always been the case, but the reason why it's so relevant right now is because of AI-assisted coding tools. While coding has always been a way to bring your ideas to life, doing so traditionally required you to actually know how to code. Even if you did, turning a random idea into something tangible could take hours, days, or even weeks.

With tools like Claude Code, Codex, and Google Antigravity, though, that barrier has become considerably lower. You no longer need to spend hours figuring out the technical side of bringing an idea to life. Instead, you can simply describe what you have in mind in plain English and let an AI coding agent handle the implementation.

You can now quite literally vibe-code anything and everything you dream of. I'm not talking about the note-taking app of your dreams that all the developers refuse to build (though you can do that, and I've done that too) or a Chrome extension that solves that one particular frustration. I'm talking about creating things that you'd probably never even associate with coding in the first place.

Crazy idea at 3 AM you'd like to see in the real world? You can build it. Want to turn an inside joke into an interactive experience that only you and your friends would understand? You can do that, too. Think interactive stories, personalized digital scrapbooks, animated birthday cards, or even an entire website dedicated to something you love. Things that don't necessarily need to exist as fully functional applications, but are simply fun to create and experiment with.

I've started using vibe coding for everything

I'm running out of reasons not to vibe-code something

Even slide decks, which have long been associated with tools like PowerPoint and Canva, where you manually drag and drop text, images, and other elements onto a slide, can now be created entirely through lines of code. With HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, you can essentially turn a presentation into an interactive experience, complete with animations, transitions, and elements that respond to what you do.

I think the above is one of the best examples I have of using vibe coding as a medium for self-expression. I've previously written about how I started vibe-coding my presentation slides instead of using traditional tools, and I haven't really looked back since. I now go all out whenever I'm creating a slide deck.

Rather than restricting myself to whatever templates or design elements a tool offers, I can describe exactly what I have in mind and let a coding agent bring it to life. The same goes for posters, which I've also started creating through vibe coding instead of relying on traditional design tools.

This idea extends to interactive simulations as well. One of my favorite examples of this was actually for a physics course I was taking last semester. For our final, we had to demonstrate a lab project we'd been working on, and I was struggling to figure out how to present our work in a way that would actually do it justice.

The obvious approach would've been to make a poster explaining the project and our findings. At most, I could've made a digital poster and presented that instead. But I really didn't want to go down that route.

So, I figured, why not create an interactive simulation instead? Rather than simply explaining how our project worked through text and images, I could actually demonstrate it in action. I used vibe coding to bring the entire thing to life, and it gave me so much more creative freedom than a traditional poster ever could.

I could experiment with how everything looked, how the simulation behaved, and how someone would interact with it. Without AI-assisted coding tools, creating something like that would've been a considerably bigger undertaking, especially alongside all my other coursework.

I've even started using vibe coding to tell stories. If there's something I want to share with a friend, more often than not, I'll find myself thinking about how I could turn it into an interactive webpage instead of simply explaining it through a bunch of messages. It's a way to show someone exactly what's going through my head, rather than hoping they picture it the same way I do.

I'm not the only one experimenting with things like this

Other people are getting creative with code, too

Zara Zhang, whom I mentioned earlier, recently created a playful interactive website dedicated entirely to the things on her wishlist. She's also built a Harry Potter-style newspaper called The Toddler Times, where the images actually come to life. These are all things that most people would probably never even think of using a coding agent for in the first place, and that's exactly what makes them so interesting!

However, I think one of the most interesting examples she's shared is of someone who turned a childhood memory of competing with their mother to kill cockroaches into a playable HTML game. According to Zhang, the person who lived through that memory actually cried when playing the game. And it wasn't because the game was particularly technically impressive. It was because of the personal story and emotions behind it.

I used Claude Code, Google Antigravity and OpenAI Codex to develop an app, and found only one worth using

Vibe coding is here to stay, and it has only one champion

33
By  Abhinav Raj

I think the above example perfectly illustrates the point I'm trying to make. Something as personal as a childhood memory can now become an interactive experience that someone else can actually play through. You don't necessarily need a business idea, a problem to solve, or even an audience. Sometimes, the story you want to tell is reason enough to build something.

item.title: Your CPU power cable is still split into 4+4 pins due to a Pentium 4-era leftover
item.itunes:title: Your CPU power cable is still split into 4+4 pins due to a Pentium 4-era leftover
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
If you look at the 8-pin cable running to the top-left corner of your motherboard, it's most likely two 4-pin cables joined together. You might even remember plugging it that way when you first assembled your PC. Almost nobody needs that split anymore, but power supplies still ship with this 4+4 split, and the reason has a lot to do with the CPU industry of the early 2000s.

Intel's Pentium 4 launched in 2000, and brought higher power requirements to desktop CPUs. This required a change in motherboard power delivery, and led to the introduction of a dedicated power cable for the CPU. From 4 pins to 4+4 pins, and later 8+4 and even 8+8 pins, the CPU power cable kept making space for increasing CPU power budgets.

The standard came about due to higher-wattage CPUs nearly three decades ago, but it continues to exist in modern power supplies and motherboards simply because there's no point in changing it.

The 24-pin ATX connector is finally getting replaced, but what comes next looks nothing like modern PC boards

Your new motherboard may look nothing like the old one, and it's mostly a good thing

18
By  Abhinav Raj

The CPU power cable wasn't always a thing

The turn of the millennium made it necessary

Credit: Source: Wikimedia Commons

Before Pentium 4 came out in 2000, all the power the motherboard needed was delivered via a single, 20-pin connector. Of course, hard drives, optical drives, and case fans needed separate cables, but the CPU (and GPU) power requirement was fulfilled by the 20-pin connector. This was the era of the original ATX standard.

When it was clear that the Pentium 4 chips needed more headroom, the ATX12V specification added a new 4-pin connector to supply +12V dedicated power to the CPU. People needed new ATX12V power supplies, while older systems continued using standard ATX models. The new 4-pin removed the burden of CPU power from the 5V rail of the main connector, making way for future redesigns.

With the ATX12V 2.0 revision in 2003, besides the main connector evolving into the 24-pin variant we know today, the 4-pin CPU connector morphed into the 4+4 pin standard most people are familiar with. It was borrowed from server motherboards to accommodate multicore CPUs with growing power requirements.

The weakest link in your PC might not be what you think

Cheap or outdated cables might be ruining your PC's safety and performance

By  Tanveer Singh

The 4+4 split solved backwards compatibility

An essential compromise

The reason manufacturers didn't simply create a rigid 8-pin CPU connector was legacy compatibility. Older motherboards still needed the regular 4-pin connector, while newer systems were quickly adopting the 4+4 pin standard. Instead of making two separate cables, they decided to ship two separate 4-pin cables. This allowed older systems to use one 4-pin cable while ignoring the other, and newer CPUs used both of them to create a fused 8-pin cable.

This EPS12V standard, borrowed from server systems, became a formal part of the ATX12V specification with the 2.2 revision around 2005. Mid-to-high wattage CPUs continued using the newer 4+4 pin standard, and the discrete design of the cable allowed consumers time to gradually adopt it without losing compatibility. As we saw in the later years, PSU standards evolved without disrupting this underlying design.

5 things you must know about your CPU's PL1, PL2, and other power limits

These power limits govern your CPU's real-world behavior

By  Tanveer Singh

Breaking the convention helps no one

Manufacturers have little incentive to change things

Just like many other conventions in the PC hardware world, the 4+4 pin split survived due to its simplicity and widespread adoption. Breaking the status quo by forcing countless systems to abruptly transition to an inflexible 8-pin standard would have helped no one. This design laid the groundwork for later developments, such as the addition of another 4-pin socket for overclocking headroom for high-wattage CPUs.

You'll see even the latest ATX 3.0 standard keep this convention unchanged. While other aspects have evolved, such as the GPU power connector, the CPU power cable split has remained mostly unchanged. Note that the 8-pin CPU and GPU cables look similar, but don't share the same pinout. Using them interchangeably can damage your hardware.

Why doesn’t Nvidia stick to 8-pin PCIe cables?

Nvidia's 12VHPWR woes still exist, making everyone think why not use 8-pin cables like before?

15
By  Tanveer Singh

Modern CPU power delivery looks a lot different

Compared to the 2000s, modern processors are a different beast. They demand way more power and are subject to a lot more algorithms and quality control issues. CPU power connectors have also evolved to keep pace with rising power budgets, but what has remained the same is the inherent logic of the connector. It still features a cable split to keep older systems in the loop, while modern PCs can leverage the newer cable standards.

item.title: Microsoft hid a Doom-like game inside Excel 31 years ago, and you can still play it
item.itunes:title: Microsoft hid a Doom-like game inside Excel 31 years ago, and you can still play it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
It's tough not to have a soft spot for easter eggs in software, especially as someone who loves finding them in video games. Things get even more endearing when developers sneak easter eggs into other, more "serious" applications. It's harmless mischief, but it makes you appreciate these tiny experiments that have become part of the collective internet lore.

As it turns out, Microsoft had some pretty interesting entries in this department. Buried inside an old version of Excel was an honest-to-goodness first-person, 3D-like game that felt like a Doom clone. This was a genuinely fun surprise for those who used it at the time, and pretty interesting to discover as a Gen-Z kid who wrongly thought that old software was nothing but jank and clunky UI.

Turns out, old software had much more personality through its quirks than modern counterparts. Even better, you can still get it running on a modern PC.

Excel had no business running a first-person game

Meet the Hall of Tortured Souls

Even though I wasn't born when Excel 95 came out, I can say for certain that making spreadsheets recalculate in Excel was never anyone's idea of a fun afternoon. Least of all, Excel wasn't the sort of software people associate with 3D gaming. And yet, Microsoft hid a little first-person adventure inside the application, aptly named the Hall of Tortured Souls.

It looked like a Doom clone, sure, but it wasn't really. Hall of Tortured Souls was a navigable 3D environment that let curious users wander around a bizarre virtual hall.

The product team never particularly advertised it, though. The easter egg was just a developer secret that you had to jump through some hoops to play. Users had to scroll down to the 95th row in a blank worksheet, select the entire row, highlight the second column, open the Help menu, and then click on About Microsoft Excel. The final step was to click the Tech Support button while holding down Ctrl+Alt+Shift, and that's what got everyone into Hall of Tortured Souls at last.

The Zelda: The Wind Waker HD PC port I've always wanted is finally here, complete with glorious 60fps

This could port soon be the definitive way to sail across the Great Sea in Wind Waker HD.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

Getting the game running on a modern PC

No, you don't need to create a virtual machine

I wasn't about to dig out a Windows 95 virtual machine to explore an Excel easter egg, so I looked for an easier way to run it. Thankfully, a GitHub repository recreates the experience using the game's decompiled source code. You can open it in VS Code and run it without resurrecting an entire vintage computing setup.

The process was refreshingly straightforward. All I had to do was grab the repository, open its folder in VS Code, build the project, and launch the game. I never needed a copy of Excel 95 or a time machine, which is nice, considering neither is particularly convenient to come by these days.

There is one rather amusing catch, though. The game is hard-coded to run in a tiny window, and there's no convenient option to scale it up. I ended up using Windows' built-in Magnifier and increasing the display scale to make the experience easier to see. It wasn't elegant, but I got the game running and had fun with it.

It ran much better on my laptop, thanks to the smaller screen and bigger scale. There's even the classic cheat code — EXCELKFA — that you can type in to access hidden hallways in the game. Fair warning, though: the game isn't some huge, sprawling dungeon crawler or arena-based shooter. It's just a nifty little thing to tell people about, play once, and that's it.

Microsoft actually had more games hidden in Office

Excel wasn't the only productivity app with secrets

Microsoft's Office Easter eggs weren't limited to Excel 95, either. Word 97 had a hidden pinball game, because apparently even writing documents wasn't enough to keep developers entertained. It was a proper little arcade distraction tucked inside a word processor, for when you got tired of typing away on the keyboard.

Excel 97 went another step further and added a whole secret flight simulator inside the spreadsheet program. It felt like a 3D plane to fly around, but the devs actually used software rendering. It had a limit on how much of the world it could render at a time, but that was par for the course for a software-based game in 1997.

These hidden extras eventually attracted scrutiny over security concerns, though, especially around undocumented code buried in productivity software. It may have seemed like harmless mischief, but it could become a headache for administrators responsible for keeping corporate systems secure.

The Pokémon: Let's Go Switch games just got a native PC port, and Nintendo probably isn't thrilled

Let's Go Recomp builds on the work that brought the Zelda: Link's Awakening remake to PC.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

The flight simulator is considerably easier to play today, since you can run a browser-based recreation in seconds without installing vintage Office. Word 97's hidden pinball game is trickier to get running, though, which makes it a little less convenient for a quick nostalgia trip.

It's ridiculous how Microsoft's old productivity suite doubled as an unofficial gaming collection. Somewhere, a spreadsheet enthusiast was just trying to balance their accounts and accidentally discovered an entirely different hobby.

Software today absolutely requires more of this quirky energy

Instead of new productivity features in tools that promise to save us another thirty seconds, I find these little software oddities much more interesting. After all, they exist because someone, somewhere, decided that building something ridiculous was worth doing. I genuinely believe that modern software could use a little more of that energy.

No, I'm not asking Microsoft to hide Unreal Engine inside the new Excel, but I'd certainly appreciate the occasional surprise that isn't a subscription prompt or an AI assistant jammed into my workflow.

Hall of Tortured Souls
See at Github

Things get even more endearing when developers sneak easter eggs into other, more "serious" applications. It's harmless mischief, but it makes you appreciate these tiny experiments that have become part of the collective internet lore.

As it turns out, Microsoft had some pretty interesting entries in this department. Buried inside an old version of Excel was an honest-to-goodness first-person, 3D-like game that felt like a Doom clone. This was a genuinely fun surprise for those who used it at the time, and pretty interesting to discover as a Gen-Z kid who wrongly thought that old software was nothing but jank and clunky UI.

Turns out, old software had much more personality through its quirks than modern counterparts. Even better, you can still get it running on a modern PC.

Excel had no business running a first-person game

Meet the Hall of Tortured Souls

Even though I wasn't born when Excel 95 came out, I can say for certain that making spreadsheets recalculate in Excel was never anyone's idea of a fun afternoon. Least of all, Excel wasn't the sort of software people associate with 3D gaming. And yet, Microsoft hid a little first-person adventure inside the application, aptly named the Hall of Tortured Souls.

It looked like a Doom clone, sure, but it wasn't really. Hall of Tortured Souls was a navigable 3D environment that let curious users wander around a bizarre virtual hall.

The product team never particularly advertised it, though. The easter egg was just a developer secret that you had to jump through some hoops to play. Users had to scroll down to the 95th row in a blank worksheet, select the entire row, highlight the second column, open the Help menu, and then click on About Microsoft Excel. The final step was to click the Tech Support button while holding down Ctrl+Alt+Shift, and that's what got everyone into Hall of Tortured Souls at last.

The Zelda: The Wind Waker HD PC port I've always wanted is finally here, complete with glorious 60fps

This could port soon be the definitive way to sail across the Great Sea in Wind Waker HD.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

Getting the game running on a modern PC

No, you don't need to create a virtual machine

I wasn't about to dig out a Windows 95 virtual machine to explore an Excel easter egg, so I looked for an easier way to run it. Thankfully, a GitHub repository recreates the experience using the game's decompiled source code. You can open it in VS Code and run it without resurrecting an entire vintage computing setup.

The process was refreshingly straightforward. All I had to do was grab the repository, open its folder in VS Code, build the project, and launch the game. I never needed a copy of Excel 95 or a time machine, which is nice, considering neither is particularly convenient to come by these days.

There is one rather amusing catch, though. The game is hard-coded to run in a tiny window, and there's no convenient option to scale it up. I ended up using Windows' built-in Magnifier and increasing the display scale to make the experience easier to see. It wasn't elegant, but I got the game running and had fun with it.

It ran much better on my laptop, thanks to the smaller screen and bigger scale. There's even the classic cheat code — EXCELKFA — that you can type in to access hidden hallways in the game. Fair warning, though: the game isn't some huge, sprawling dungeon crawler or arena-based shooter. It's just a nifty little thing to tell people about, play once, and that's it.

Microsoft actually had more games hidden in Office

Excel wasn't the only productivity app with secrets

Microsoft's Office Easter eggs weren't limited to Excel 95, either. Word 97 had a hidden pinball game, because apparently even writing documents wasn't enough to keep developers entertained. It was a proper little arcade distraction tucked inside a word processor, for when you got tired of typing away on the keyboard.

Excel 97 went another step further and added a whole secret flight simulator inside the spreadsheet program. It felt like a 3D plane to fly around, but the devs actually used software rendering. It had a limit on how much of the world it could render at a time, but that was par for the course for a software-based game in 1997.

These hidden extras eventually attracted scrutiny over security concerns, though, especially around undocumented code buried in productivity software. It may have seemed like harmless mischief, but it could become a headache for administrators responsible for keeping corporate systems secure.

The Pokémon: Let's Go Switch games just got a native PC port, and Nintendo probably isn't thrilled

Let's Go Recomp builds on the work that brought the Zelda: Link's Awakening remake to PC.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

The flight simulator is considerably easier to play today, since you can run a browser-based recreation in seconds without installing vintage Office. Word 97's hidden pinball game is trickier to get running, though, which makes it a little less convenient for a quick nostalgia trip.

It's ridiculous how Microsoft's old productivity suite doubled as an unofficial gaming collection. Somewhere, a spreadsheet enthusiast was just trying to balance their accounts and accidentally discovered an entirely different hobby.

Software today absolutely requires more of this quirky energy

Instead of new productivity features in tools that promise to save us another thirty seconds, I find these little software oddities much more interesting. After all, they exist because someone, somewhere, decided that building something ridiculous was worth doing. I genuinely believe that modern software could use a little more of that energy.

No, I'm not asking Microsoft to hide Unreal Engine inside the new Excel, but I'd certainly appreciate the occasional surprise that isn't a subscription prompt or an AI assistant jammed into my workflow.

item.title: A single roll of PETG has fixed more things around my house than my entire toolbox
item.itunes:title: A single roll of PETG has fixed more things around my house than my entire toolbox
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Whether you’re planning to print cool-looking models, cosplay props, or just regular ol’ replacement parts for your household accessories, you’ll want to be careful with your filament of choice – and that’s a lesson I learned only after leaving a PLA model in direct sunlight and finding its deformed remains the next day. Since then, I’ve tinkered with different filaments over the course of my 3D printing journey, and after realizing their perks and quirks, I’ve developed a preference for certain materials.

For example, I always keep a TPU roll for wearable components and projects that require high-elasticity models. Then there’s PETG, which I’ve used for the majority of my 3D prints after I began printing practical accessories instead of aesthetically-pleasing models.

7 reasons I’m switching to PETG filament for my 3D printing

While PLA filament is best for 3D printing beginners, there are strong advantages to using PETG instead

11
By  Jeff Butts

PETG is durable enough for most functional prints in my house

It’s better than PLA for printing everyday items

One of the best aspects of PETG, aside from its affordable nature, is that it’s durable enough for utility prints that I don’t want to replace every few months. For one, PETG has rock-solid impact resistance, and since it flexes under heavy load instead of shattering, it’s safe enough for hooks, clips, and mounting brackets that get exposed to mechanical stress. It also has better heat tolerance than regular PLA, making it perfect for my DIY accessories designed for outdoor use or the insides of my PCs.

Better yet, PETG models are fairly resistant to water, oils, and common chemicals, so I can use them for garage tools, garden equipment, and even bathroom accessories without worrying about the prints becoming unusable in a few days.

I typically use PETG for most of my home lab prints

Heck, it's the sole reason I was able to organize cable chaos in my tinkering cave

Switching to the practical side of my 3D printing escapades, my home lab is where I spend the majority of my time working on DIY projects, and I used PETG for pretty much every model in my tech cave. Take my cable organization setup, for example. Since PETG can handle mechanical stress, it’s what I used when creating cable clips that route wires by latching along the sides of my desk, and the same applies to my under-desk trays. I’ve also printed PETG mounting brackets for cheap network switches and WAPs, and they’ve held up perfectly well for months.

Likewise, PETG is reliable enough to withstand the heat within my gaming PC and servers, which is why I used it to design snap-on wire clips. In fact, I even created a custom PSU shroud for one of my old PC cases to hide some of the cable clutter. PETG drive caddies work just as well for my NAS rigs and DIY storage servers, and I’m already planning to put together a custom DAS that uses PETG for the chassis and typical physical components.

But it’s just as useful for custom accessories and replacement parts

I even use it for home organization frameworks and gardening tools

Besides my home lab, PETG has been a reliable companion for the rest of my household accessories. Although I’m too wary of using any kind of PETG rolls (including the safe variants) for food containers, it’s great for jar organizers and bag-sealing accessories. Since PETG is fairly resistant to moisture after I turn the filament into tangible models, I’ve also used it to create toothpaste squeezers, detergent racks, and phone mounts for my bathroom. On the gardening front, it works well for hose splitters, pot trays, and plant labels.

I also use PETG extensively when creating knobs, latch components, retention pins, and other replacement parts. Heck, it’s pretty effective for creating replacement components for tech devices, like the MIPI latch on my Raspberry Pi 5 and custom hoses for my vacuum cleaner.

That said, PETG has a handful of quirks

So far, I’ve only discussed PETG’s utility in my household 3D prints, but this robust filament isn’t without its problems. And I’m not just talking about the glossy finish on PETG prints, either. Although my PETG prints aren’t very vulnerable to water, the filament itself is a different story. Since it’s hygroscopic, a semi-used roll can absorb quite a bit of moisture if I leave the spool hanging on my 3D printer. Of course, it’s not really a problem when I have print queues for massive models that can drain an entire spool worth of filament.

But since most of my everyday objects (and I’ll discuss this in a bit) take up anywhere between 10g to 75g, I have to be extremely careful when handling freshly-opened spools or risk dealing with excessive stringing. In fact, the humidity in my backwater town is so high that I ended up getting a filament dryer and several desiccant packets just to preserve my newly-opened spools.

5 filaments that are better than PLA for serious 3D printing projects

While PLA definitely fills the 3D printing needs for many projects, other filament materials are better for more serious projects

8
By  Jeff Butts
